abstract: The origin of life on Earth occurred within a narrow window delimited by cessation of intense late accretion bombardment at about 4.4 Ga on the one hand, and younger evidence gleaned via molecular phylogenetic studies, isotopic biosignatures and morphological traces on the other. Molecular clock analyses tentatively place the median age for the Last Universal Common Ancestor LUCA population of all contemporary DNA life at about 4.2 Ga. Cryptic isotopic biosignatures go back as far as 4.1 Ga in Hadean zircons and more robustly in Eoarchean rocks at about 3.83 Ga. Morphological remains including microfossils and microbially mediated sedimentary structures are almost as ancient, around 3.5 Ga. To make better sense of this early and rapid timeline and its implications for a biosphere on Hadean Earth, we parameterize the kinetic windows for that transition from non-living to living chemistry, abiogenesis. Here, we reinforce the finding that before the LUCA, a RiboNucleic Acid RNA and RiboNucleoProtein RNP World could have persisted for less than 130 Myr. Furthermore, we show that conditions which define the kinetic windows for early Earth stand out compared to other worlds in our Solar System considered as candidates for abiogenesis. Specifically, these are sustained stable liquid water from 4.4 Ga, wet-dry cycling on dry land under an atmosphere, effective crustal recycling to rejuvenate disequilibrium chemistry, available key elements for synthesis and growth, mechanisms to concentrate prebiotic reaction products without also destroying them, and sufficient spatial scales for subsequent evolution and diversification. We argue that the steps from abiogenesis to DNA required chemistry coordinated with environmental conditions overlapping in time with each transition from prebiotic synthesis to cellular life governed by distinct rate limiting processes operating over geologically short timescales. Our analysis suggests that if DNA life had not emerged, an informationally deficient and thermally unstable RNA biosphere would eventually have gone extinct.
